title: Hybrid GPU Bursting: Cloud + Edge Pool Patterns and Runbook
author: Asha Patel
content:
Summary:
This document describes recommended patterns, Terraform/IaC modules, and an operational runbook for hybrid GPU bursting: dynamically offloading overflow inference and training traffic from Redwood’s core cloud GPU pools to short-lived cloud/edge pools. The goal is predictable latency and cost control during traffic spikes while preserving tenant isolation and auditability.

Scope:
- Applies to public-hosted and Dedicated customer workloads that allow bursting (customer opt-in).
- Covers design patterns, IaC snippets, autoscaling triggers, network/egress considerations, security, cost guardrails, test plan, and oncall procedures.
- Excludes long-running migration of baseline workloads (see capacity-reservation docs).

Motivation:
As model-serving traffic is spiky, static reserved pools lead to wasted committed capacity or missed requests. Hybrid bursting lets us:
- Keep predictable baseline latency using dedicated pools.
- Meet short-term spikes with ephemeral capacity in other cloud regions or edge provider pools.
- Limit cost via placement policies and pre-configured eviction/teardown policies.

Key concepts and definitions:
- Baseline pool: Reserved, SLA-backed GPU pool (Dedicated or protected host group).
- Burst pool: Ephemeral GPU fleet (spot/ephemeral instances, on-demand in other region, or edge partner nodes).
- Placement policy: Rules that determine where requests route (latency-first, cost-first, regulatory-first).
- Eviction policy: Criteria to tear down burst nodes (max-runtime, idle-time, cost-threshold).

Architecture patterns (three recommended flavors):
1) Regional Cloud Burst (fastest to implement)
- Trigger: baseline_utilization > 85% for 30s
- Provision: Cloud autoscaling group in secondary region with identical runtime image + network peering
- Use-case: high-throughput inference where additional regional latency is tolerable
- Tradeoffs: cross-region egress, cold-start delay ~30–90s

2) Spot/Ephemeral Spot Fleet Burst (cost-optimized)
- Trigger: baseline_cost_per_token > target_cost * 1.2 OR baseline_utilization > 90%
- Provision: spot instances in same region with strict eviction policy and cached models to reduce warmup
- Use-case: throughput spikes with short tail latency tolerance and can accept 1–5% token loss/retry
- Tradeoffs: potential preemption; requires fast fallback to baseline model variants

3) Edge Partner Burst (low added latency for specific customers)
- Trigger: customer_tier == enterprise && baseline_latency > SLO
- Provision: edge partner pool in customer-preferred geography with VPC peering or private link
- Use-case: geo-sensitive, low-latency customer traffic spikes
- Tradeoffs: higher per-hour cost; contract and audit controls required

Routing and fallback policy examples:
- Primary policy: route to Baseline pool while utilization < 80% and per-request latency < 120ms (p50).
- Secondary policy: if Baseline_utilization >= 80% or p95_latency >= 200ms, route to Burst pool tagged cost:low first, region:nearest second.
- Fallback policy: if Burst pool fails to provision or returns errors > 3%, fallback to degraded-mode: reduce max_output_tokens by 25% and route to baseline.

Security and networking considerations:
- All burst pools must register via the same control-plane identity (OIDC client) and use mTLS to service mesh gateway.
- Egress constraints: apply egress NAT gateways with per-pool bandwidth limits. For cross-region bursts, enable per-customer egress budgets to avoid surprise bills.
- VPC peering: use dedicated peering connections for enterprise edge bursts; default to shared transit for region-to-region bursts.
- IAM: burst pools limited to model-serving roles only; no access to customer data stores except via audited read-only service account with short-lived tokens.

Terraform/IaC patterns (snippets):
- Module layout recommended:
  - modules/gpu-burst/variables.tf (placement, instance_profile, max_count, provider_alias)
  - modules/gpu-burst/main.tf (asg/instance template, user-data to pull runtime bundle)
  - modules/gpu-burst/outputs.tf (node_pool_id, sg_ids)

Example (pseudocode) for module invocation:
```hcl
module "gpu_burst_eu_west" {
  source        = "git::ssh://git@repo/path/modules/gpu-burst.git"
  providers     = { aws = aws.eu_west }
  placement     = "region:eu-west-1,type:spot"
  max_count     = 40
  instance_type = "g5.xlarge"
  iam_role      = module.roles.gpu_burst_role.arn
  cost_limit    = 1200 # USD per day for this pool
}
```

User-data example to speed warmup (bash snippet):
```bash
#!/bin/bash
set -e
# warm model cache and runtime kernel selection
sudo systemctl start redwood-runtime
/opt/redwood/bin/preload-model --model-id ${MODEL_ID} --kv-cache-enabled
```

Autoscaling and SLO knobs to configure in controller (example keys):
- scale_up_threshold: 0.85
- scale_down_threshold: 0.25
- min_nodes: 0
- max_nodes: 50
- cooldown_seconds: 45
- warmup_timeout_seconds: 90

Costs and guardrails:
- Per-pool cost_limit enforced by controller; when approaching 90% of daily budget, take aggressive scale-in and/or change placement to cheaper spot fleet.
- Billing alert: send alert when projected_monthly_burst_spend > 20% of customer_contract_commit.
- Quotas: each org can have at most 3 concurrent burst pools without explicit approval.

Testing and validation plan before rollout:
1) Canary in a sandbox with synthetic traffic patterns: 1h soak at 1.5x baseline QPS, check p50/p95 latency and error rate
2) Preemption simulation for spot pools: issue orchestrated SIGTERM to 10% nodes and validate fallback
3) Cross-region cold-start test: measure cold-start 5/50/95 percentiles; ensure warmup reduces median startup below 40s
4) Cost throttle test: trigger cost_limit and verify graceful scale-in and traffic throttling behavior

Operational runbook (step-by-step):
1) Detection
   - Trigger condition: Baseline pool p95_latency > 200ms OR Baseline_utilization > 85% for 60s.
   - Alerts to #infra-gpu-bursting and oncall phone.
2) Automated remediation (first 2 minutes)
   - Controller attempts to provision burst pool per placement policy.
   - If provision succeeds: mark pool active and route 20% of new requests to it, ramp to 100% over 2 minutes.
3) If provisioning fails (after 2 attempts / 3 minutes):
   - Runbook step: oncall runs `infractl burst describe --pool <id>` and checks cloud account quotas and VPC peering state.
   - Common fixes: increase subnet ip pool, approve quota request, refresh transit gateway route tables.
4) Degraded mode: if errors persist 5+ minutes, enable degraded-mode for affected customers (reduce max tokens, increase temperature floor) and open incident ticket.
5) Post-incident: run incident review, attach telemetry (allocation timeline, cost delta, logs) and open action items for any IaC changes.

Escalation matrix and ownership:
- Tier 1 (oncall infra): attempt automated fixes, follow runbook; if unable to restore within 15 minutes escalate to Tier 2.
- Tier 2 (network/iaas engineer): check cloud quota, VPC peering, NAT throughput, and Terraform plans for drift.
- Tier 3 (runtime/serving lead): investigate scheduler, model cache warmup, and fallback policy tuning.
Contact list:
- infra-oncall: #infra-oncall Slack channel (pager duty)
- network-owners: network@redwood.ai
- runtime-team: runtime@redwood.ai

Health metrics to monitor (minimum):
- burst_provision_latency_seconds (histogram)
- baseline_pool_utilization (gauge)
- burst_pool_capacity (gauge)
- request_routing_errors_total (counter)
- cost_spent_today_usd (gauge)
- per_customer_egress_bytes (gauge)

Exported dashboards and alerts (recommended thresholds):
| Metric | Alert threshold | Owner | Escalation |
| baseline_pool_utilization | > 85% for 60s | infra-oncall | Tier1 |
| burst_provision_latency_seconds{p95} | > 180s | infra-oncall | Tier2 |
| request_routing_errors_total | > 5% of requests in 5m | runtime | Tier2 |
| cost_spent_today_usd / projected_daily_budget | > 0.9 | finance-infra | Ops-lead |
Runbook postmortem checklist (minimum items to include):
- Timeline of events with timestamps
- Which placement policy used and why
- Warmup behavior and cache hit rate change
- Cost delta and impacted customers
- Action items: IaC changes, monitoring additions, policy adjustments

Operational constraints and known limitations:
- Cold-starts remain the largest contributor to p95 latency during cross-region bursts. Pre-warm images and model caches where possible.
- Spot preemption can cause transient 429s; ensure client retry/backoff is configured.
- Edge partner bursts require legal review and an enterprise contract; do not enable for free-tier customers.

Appendix: Useful commands and debugging tips:
- Describe pool: `infractl pool describe --id <pool-id> --format yaml`
- Force scale-up: `infractl pool scale --id <pool-id> --count 10`
- Check VPC peering: `aws ec2 describe-vpc-peering-connections --filters Name=tag:Pool,Values=<pool-id>`
- Simulate traffic spike: `wrk -t8 -c200 -d300s http://runtime-proxy/synthesize?rate_multiplier=1.8`

Appendix: Short lived feature flags and rollback knobs:
- Feature flag: `enable_hybrid_bursting_v2` (default: false). If rollout introduces instability set to false and traffic will remain on baseline only.
- Rollback: disable feature flag + `infractl pool delete --selector placement=burst` to tear down active burst pools.
